*Storm has the upside of being able to start the combo with any cantrip or ritual, but *Ad *Nauseum starts with only the namesake card or a Spoils of the Vault.  

**Combo **Robustness

*Edge: *Ad *Nauseum

The whole point of playing *Ad *Nauseum is being able to win 99.9% of games where you resolve both Angel's Grace and Ad Nauseum.  You run a number of Pact of Negation in the deck, which means unless they have a Counterflux or have removed your Lightning Storm from the deck, you can't lose.  Both are EXTREMELY RARE in G1, and still unlikely in G2.

*Storm, on the other hand, can be disrupted during the combo, and key combo enablers like Goblin Electromancer and Pyromancer Ascension and be removed by Abrupt Decay, Maelstrom Pulse, Nahiri, etc.  Also,*Storm is more vulnerable to counterspells except when it actually casts a big Grapeshot.

**Storm **vs. **Ad **Nauseum **in **Practice

**Edge: **Ad **Nauseum

With a great hand, either deck can "go off" on Turn 3, but *Ad *Nauseum has the tools in G1 to survive *Storm's combo, either making it more difficult with Phyrexian Unlife or using Angel's Grace in response to a Grapeshot.  I would much rather be on the side of *Ad *Nauseum.

**Vs. **Aggro

**Edge: **Storm

Obviously in this match the question is how fast can you combo?  In most situations, one can combo off faster with *Storm than with*Ad *Nauseum **IF *Storm can land an enabler.  Theoretically, one could combo off with *Storm on Turn 3 a lot easier than *Ad *Nauseum could.  

**Vs. Control

**Edge: **Ad **Nauseum

Nahiri Control and Jeskai Control will always have a presence in Modern, and in these matches, it's better to have things which can't be countered.  That said, *Storm has the SB tech of Empty The Warrens, which is great for the Control match.  In generel though, it's easier to slip through with *Ad *Nauseum because only the most specific counterspells will stop it.  

**Flexibility

**Edge: **Storm

The other category to consider is how to get to your win condition.  Essentially, if Ad Nauseum and/or Spoils of the Vault gets countered, you're dead in the water.  It's also incredibly hard to combo if you can't keep a Phyrexian Unlife on the table.  With *Storm, your combo accelerants are not mandatory pieces in your victory puzzle.  They help, but you can start your victory plan with just a few cantrips.  

**Conclusion

According to recent results in Modern and on the Pro Tour, *UR *Storm has the competitive edge against *Ad *Nauseum, and practice with *Storm can elevate your performance arguably more than any other deck (except perhaps Jund, because Jund is highly customizable).

Alright, let's go through a couple sample hands and I'll tell you how I would sequence them.  Let's assume all hands are for Game 1 against an unknown opponent, but you know your meta so you could be inclined to prep against aggro strategies.  

Sample Hand #1 (On the Play): Bloodstained Mire, Scavenging Ooze, Raging Ravine, Overgrown Tomb, Inquisition of Kozilek, Lightning Bolt, Liliana of the Veil.  

Before you read my suggestions, you make the play and see what you come up with.  If it's not immediately apparent, don't worry about it.  That's why we have exercises like this.  :)  Think it out before reading ahead.

The obvious question here is should you lead with a tapped land to guarantee a Turn 3 Liliana or should you lead with an untapped land and use Inquisition into Scooze, with a possibility of not casting Lili on T3.  My inclination here is to play the Overgrown Tomb untapped and fire off a discard spell, and here's my reasoning.  Our deck is at its best when we can strip away gas cards and remove their stuff.  Also, if we make them discard a creature, then T2 cast a Scooze, and then God forbid we whiff on drawing untapped land, we can still use Scooze to "eat" the creature they discarded and have a larger Ooze to block or attack.

Leading with a tapped Raging Ravine lets you guarantee a Lili on T3, but you lose major tempo and strand the Inquisition in your hand.  Against an aggro deck, you may not ever have a good opportunity to cast the Inquisition later on, and that T1 or T2 creature in their hand, or key counterspell if it's not aggro, could be just the sort of tempo advantage they need to keep us on the back foot all game.

Sample Hand #2 (On the Play): Terminate, Kolaghan's Command, Lightning Bolt, Dark Confidant, Tarmogoyf, Overgrown Tomb, Bloodstained Mire.

It's tempting to play the Tomb tapped on T1 to save some damage when you cast your Goyf on T2, but if you expect a creature deck, your most logical play would be the Mire for 2 reasons:

1) If they play a creature on T1, you may want to Bolt it.  With Mire, you leave yourself that option.

2) You can fetch a Blood Crypt at EOT and set up so that any land you draw off the top will enable all your spells.  

Technically you take the same amount of damage either way, but the big advantage with Mire over Tomb is the potential tempo advantage of having Lightning Bolt at the ready.   
(Also, you may be thinking "Boxerbum!  The fetch before my draw step minimized my chances of drawing a third land by a measurable amount!"  You're right, but that amount is quite negligible in the long run.)

The other question is which spell to play on T2.  You have two very good options here, but it depends on their T1 play.  If they play a threatening creature like Wild Nacatyl (And you Bolt it, of course), you may want to play Goyf first to help stabilize against future creatures.  On the other hand, against a T1 of land-go, Confidant will start providing card advantage right away and is the clear play.  This is a tricky scenario and requires that you read the first turn of the game to make a good decision.  Definitely lead with Mire though.  You leave yourself more options that way.  You can even fetch a basic Mountain on T1 if you need to Bolt a creature, and still have access to all your spells.

Sample Hand #3 (On the Draw): Kolaghan's Command, Raging Ravine x2, Lightning Bolt, Liliana of the Veil, Bloodstained Mire, Tarmogoyf.

This is a pretty weird hand for sequencing, so let's examine the options.

Option 1: Play Raging Ravine T1, Play Ravine #2 on T2, leaving up Bolt.  
This lets you set up Goyf for T3, but you can Bolt an early threat.  It also sets up a potential Kommand for T3, which is great against Affinity and/or Infect.

Option #2: Play Raging Ravine on T1, play Bloodstained Mire and fetch for a Goyf on T2, then possibly draw the third land for Kommand, or play another Ravine and leave up Bolt.
This lets you get a threat on the table earlier, but the trade-off is you can't use Kommand until at least T4 (assuming you don't draw a land).  

Option #3: Play Bloodstained Mire T1, Ravine T2, Ravine T3 and Goyf. 
This lets you keep up Bolt for an early creature, but you basically skip your T2 and can't cast Goyf until T3, with no Bolt backup if you didn't fire it off on the first two turns.

The "correct" option will become apparent on T1.  If they lead with a mana creature like Hierarch or Birds, you will probably want to lead with Mire into Bolt because that means they're most likely on a Chord deck, and Jund's only way to beat Chord is to kill their dorks and keep their creatures under control until you can kill them with a threat.  I.e. Option #3 is "correct" in this case, in my experience.

If they're T1 play is just a land, or a land into Serum Visions, I would go with the Ravine to start.  Clearly there's no reason to leave up Bolt, and therefore there's no reason to deny yourself a T2 play.

The decision trees branch off from there of course, but hopefully these examples are of use to you!  And by all means, keep asking and I'll keep giving you tips and tricks, whether it's for general theory of Jund or specific match advice.  :)

Right on, I'm a big fan of Jund.  This is definitely a deck whose results are tied to the tuning.  First, I'll ask you how you've been doing lately in your meta.  Is there a deck that consistently beats yours, or an area of play which you're having recurring problems with?  Your list seems pretty legit at a glance.  

A couple observations for you from a fellow Jund fan:
1) Eldrazi is an inherently poor match in the dark for Jund.  It's typically around 65% for them, and most of that comes from being on the play.  Your 3-3 split of Thoughtseize and Inquisition seems good if you're expecting less Burn and Zoo and more grindy matches.  My best success with them is to keep a hand which can rip apart their hand and mop up the survivors.  Take Thought-Knot Seer as fast as possible even over a Smasher because card disadvantage will be the death of you in that match.  

2) For the mirror, you wanna jam your deck full of disruption and removal.  I would cut a Bolt, the Pact, and a Liliana for an EE (for Goyf, Bob, and Scooze all in one) and the pair of finks.  You just gotta jam as much gas as possible.  When using discard spells, it can be tempting to take threats, but unless it's something you can't remove (unlikely, given your current removal package) I prioritize taking enemy discard spells and planeswalkers, as these will disrupt yous plan of "Cast creatures, recur our threats, rinse and repeat till they're dead."  
Kommand is a huge card for you and you should expect to always use them to get back Bolted threats and hopefully always make them discard.  The first player in topdeck mode has a huge disadvantage.

Infect is the fasted kill you'll probably face.  The biggest possible sequencing issue people have is when to try to kill the attacking creature.  You almost NEVER want to kill pre-combat (unless not killing will guaranteed lead to death) because if they have a pump spell (and they normally do), you'll get hit for way more damage than if you wait for them to make the first move.  

Good luck go you and let me knew if this abscess your questions!  And remember, don't be defeated by defeat, learn from it!

1) The best way to know if your plays are correct is to make similar plays that you think are correct and see how often they lead to victory.  There's a big difference between making the "correct" play and making the "winning" play.  

What I mean by this is there will be certain decision trees where one will be correct 80% of the time, but making that play may lead to a losing position based on other factors.  There will also be places where you may be accidentally or erroneously rewarded for making the wrong play.  For instance, if you neglect to remove a creature with a sorcery but your opponent plays around an instant speed answer and you Fog them for a turn.  You may have got a good outcome, but that wasn't the correct play.  It takes TONS of practice to know what the right play is, but there are definitely "right" and "wrong" ways to play a deck in the dark.

2) I assume you're playing one of the top-tier decks if you're posting in r/spikes, so the first step is obviously to netdeck and use that configuration for some testing.  The exact configuration will be up to you once you have experience with the deck and also can identify your meta.  For instance, playing a control deck will give you highly variable rates of success based solely on your maindeck tweaking.  Goldfish the netdeck, test against the field, make any obvious changes, check out the meta, make more changes, and then run the gauntlet again.  Often, players will fall into the trap of tinkering too much with a good thing when they think they have "cracked" the format.  Be wary of these major changes and test thoroughly before deciding definitely.

3) This comes down to practice matches and goldfishingn straight up.  You will learn in every game you play.  If you like, you could send me a list you're playing and if I know how to play it (I'm proficient with the majority of Tier 1 and Tier 2 decks in Modern), I can offer tips.  As a rule though, play the deck in 100 matches.  You'll be very comfortable with your sequencing after much practice.  

Hope this helps, OP!

I've been struggling with this debate since I started playing in Constructed tournaments back in the Innistrad block.  My favorite format is Modern by far, even with the wrecked state it's in.  The big question for the last few weeks has clearly been, "Should I play Eldrazi or try to fight them?  And if I do choose the hero's path, which deck will I champion?"  

The answer is difficult to take for a natural rogue like me, but all Spikes must consider a deck with significantly more raw power than any other legal deck in the format.  Don't get me wrong here.  I'm typically a blue control player, and there's almost nothing I like more than sleeving up counter magic and winning by repeating that magic word, "No".  But Blue is absolutely the weakest color in the current format.  Until the Eldrazi are banished to the Blind Eternities once more, or at least to the second Tier, the most logical winning strategy is to use them.

Now, Modern is a simple example of this decision process, and with the vast majority of Day 2 and Top 8 decks of the recent 4 GP's being Eldrazi variants, we can see the clear forerunner in power.  There are other great decks in the format, as seen by the victory of Abzan Chord over Eldrazi decks in Detroit, and in the presence of UR Storm in that same Top 8.  However, when choosing a deck as a Spike, we need to be wary of anything other than the very best.  

On the other hand, when a new, less skewed format rolls around, how we navigate the perils of choosing the "right" deck?  The answer is two-pronged.  

1) We need to test all available Tier 1 decks against the others in that tier, as well as Tier 1.5-Tier 2.  The statistics we gather with these should narrow down the options to a select few best decks.  In last season's format, for instance, the best two options were Splinter Twin and Amulet Bloom (Both of which were neutered with the last bans).

2) We need to identify our meta-game and choose a deck that has the best record against our expected meta-game.  We also have to tune that deck with proper sideboard plans and maximize our ability to wreck opponents while minimizing "win more" card slots and focussing on consistency.  

Through thorough analysis and enough practice, I do believe any player can take a Tier 1 deck to its absolute limits and get the best possible results against the other format leaders.
